hook: Your town has one empty lot. Some residents want a park, store owners want a parking garage, and a grocery chain wants to lease it. Everyone has a good reason, and there is only one lot. That single, ordinary problem, more wants than resources, is where all of economics starts.

prereq.why: Only a change off the axes shifts a curve.

figure.caption: Unlimited wants and limited resources create scarcity, which forces every society to choose what to produce, how and for whom.

chain.cause: People's wants are unlimited, but land, labor, capital and entrepreneurship are limited

chain.effect: every person, firm and government must choose how to use them

chain.cause: Choosing one use of a resource
chain.effect: means giving up another use: a trade-off

chain.cause: A whole society faces those choices
chain.effect: its economic system decides what to produce, how and for whom

ideas: Scarcity: wants are greater than the resources to meet them. It applies to rich and poor, and to time as well as money.
The four factors of production: land (natural resources), labor (human effort), capital (tools, machines, buildings) and entrepreneurship (organizing and risk-taking). Money is not one of them.
Every choice is a trade-off: using a resource one way means not using it another way.
Market, command and mixed economic systems answer what, how and for whom in different ways; most real economies are mixed.

misconception.wrong: Money is capital, so a business that borrows money has gained a factor of production.
misconception.right: In economics, capital means made goods used to produce other goods, such as machines and buildings. Money buys factors of production but is not one itself.

summary: Scarcity means wants are greater than the resources to meet them, so every person, business and government must choose, and every choice is a trade-off. The resources are the four factors of production: land, labor, capital and entrepreneurship. A society's economic system, market, command or mixed, decides what to produce, how to produce it and for whom; most real economies mix markets with some government roles.
